title: The Lantern and the Salt: Cheapside, the Dead Sea, and the Crypt of St Paul's
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Wood Street, Cheapside: the warehouse manager's son
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the second of April a son is born in Wood Street, Cheapside, to William Hunt, manager of a City warehouse, and his wife Sarah, born Hobman. The street runs a few minutes from St Paul's, whose crypt will hold his ashes eighty-three years later. The family is not poor and not connected; it deals in goods, not pictures, and expects the boy to do the same. The Royal Academy Schools have been teaching in London for nearly sixty years by the time he is born, and they will refuse him twice before they let him in.
suggested_refs: Wood Street, Cheapside, in the City of London, half a mile from St Paul's Cathedral

stops.name: Ewell, the clerk's misspelling
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the baptism at St Mary the Virgin, Ewell is attested by family tradition relayed in Wikipedia, but no source reached this session gives its date. May 1827 is a placeholder inside the birth year.
stops.campa: He is baptised at St Mary the Virgin in Ewell, and a clerk writing out the register spells his mother's maiden name wrong: Hobman becomes Holman. Later he takes the error for his own and signs it, so that the name the world knows him by is a scribal accident preserved on purpose. The date of the baptism is not recorded in anything reachable. What survives is the mechanism and the choice: a painter who will insist for sixty years on copying exactly what stands in front of him keeps, as his middle name, a copying mistake.
suggested_refs: The parish registers of St Mary the Virgin, Ewell, Surrey
sources: Wikipedia, 'William Holman Hunt' (family tradition, not independently documented)

stops.name: Cheapside, the clerk's stool
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year band; the DNB places the move in his thirteenth year, so 1839 or 1840
stops.campa: In his thirteenth year he is taken out of school and set to earn. First he assists a surveyor and estate agent; then he goes to the London agency of Richard Cobden, calico printer and free-trader, where the ledgers concern cloth. He draws in whatever hours the desk leaves him. Twice the Royal Academy Schools refuse him, and twice he goes back to the ledgers. The third application goes in from the same stool, made by a clerk who has taught himself to draw between columns of figures.
suggested_refs: The London agency of Richard Cobden, calico printer, where Hunt clerked as a boy
sources: Dictionary of National Biography, 1912 supplement, 'Hunt, William Holman'

stops.name: Trafalgar Square, the Royal Academy Schools admit him
stops.date_confidence: the 1844 admission is attested; the location of the Schools in the National Gallery building rests on standard biographies and was not verified against a document this session
stops.campa: The Schools occupy part of the National Gallery building on the north side of Trafalgar Square, and in 1844 they admit him as a probationer at the third asking. He is seventeen. Here he meets John Everett Millais, four years younger and already a prodigy, admitted at eleven. The two become allies before they become anything else. Which building on the square housed the Schools in that year rests on the standard biographies rather than on a document reached, and is carried here as reconstruction.
stops.quote: Long years are needed to train the eye and hand before a man can represent on a flat surface any forms of creation under the simplest conditions.
stops.quote_source: William Holman Hunt, Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (Macmillan, 1905), Preface
suggested_refs: The Royal Academy Schools in their National Gallery premises, Trafalgar Square, 1844
sources: Diana Holman-Hunt, My Grandfather, His Wives and Loves (1969), as relayed; not consulted directly

stops.name: Royal Academy, Little Nell and the resurrection morning
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: In 1845 he paints Little Nell and Her Grandfather, taken from The Old Curiosity Shop, a novel five years old whose author is alive and working across London. In 1847 he paints a first version of Christ and the Two Marys. The two subjects, a popular novelist and the resurrection morning, mark out between them the ground he will work for the rest of his life: whatever the age is reading, painted with the seriousness the age reserves for scripture. He is a student still and exhibits as one.
suggested_refs: Hunt's Little Nell and Her Grandfather (1845) and the first Christ and the Two Marys (1847)

stops.name: Cleveland Street, the shared lodging
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period; Wikipedia gives the sharing as c. 1848, without months
stops.campa: He takes rooms on Cleveland Street in Fitzrovia with Dante Gabriel Rossetti, a year his junior, a poet who paints and a painter who cannot yet draw. Rossetti has come to him as a pupil after seeing a picture. They work in the same light and argue in the same room, and the argument, in the year before the Brotherhood is named, is about whether English painting has anything left in it. Neither has sold anything of consequence. Between them they decide the answer is no, and go on painting on that basis.
stops.quote: If the open road ended in an impassable waste, we had to make a new way; it might be to push through the forest darkness, to root out venomous undergrowth, to substitute wholesome stock.
stops.quote_source: William Holman Hunt, Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (Macmillan, 1905), Preface
suggested_refs: The Cleveland Street lodgings shared by Hunt and Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Fitzrovia

stops.name: Royal Academy, The Eve of St Agnes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; May is the Academy's exhibition month, not a documented date
stops.campa: He shows The Eve of St Agnes at the Academy exhibition, a Keats subject at a moment when Keats is twenty-seven years dead and not yet safely canonical. Rossetti stands in front of it, praises it aloud in the room, and comes to find the painter. Hunt is the one with the training and the trade; Rossetti is the one with the manifesto temperament and a brother who will keep minutes. Within four months there will be a Brotherhood with a secret set of initials.
stops.quote: Rossetti enthusiastic over my picture. Proposes to come and see me. He visits my studio. Confesses being disheartened at his position.
stops.quote_source: William Holman Hunt, Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (Macmillan, 1905), chapter-heading synopsis; a contents line, not verified as running prose
suggested_refs: Hunt's The Eve of St Agnes at the Royal Academy exhibition of 1848

stops.name: 83 Gower Street, the seven and the three letters
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1848; the day is not given
stops.campa: In the Millais family house on Gower Street, seven young men agree to call themselves the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood: Hunt, Millais, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, and with them William Michael Rossetti, James Collinson, Frederic George Stephens, Thomas Woolner. They mean by the name that English painting went wrong after Raphael and must be taken back behind him. Thirty-nine years earlier in Rome, Johann Friedrich Overbeck and the Lukasbund had made the same argument in German and moved into a monastery to prove it. The English version keeps its day jobs and signs its canvases PRB.
stops.quote: Our purpose was formed with deliberation, and we had such faith in our initial thought that we disdained caution in our plans.
stops.quote_source: William Holman Hunt, Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (Macmillan, 1905), Preface
suggested_refs: 83 Gower Street, Bloomsbury, the Millais family house, today the Arosfa Hotel

stops.name: Royal Academy, Rienzi and the secret spelled out
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; May is the Academy's exhibition month
stops.campa: Rienzi goes to the Academy in 1849 signed with three letters nobody outside the seven can read. The Haunted Manor is finished the same year. In January 1850 the Brotherhood begins printing its own magazine, The Germ, which runs four issues to April and stops. Then a newspaper prints what PRB stands for, and a secret society becomes a target with a name. The reviews turn. Hunt has spent his working life to that point on the proposition that exactness is a moral act, and the press has decided that exactness is an affront.
stops.quote: A newspaper publishes the secret of the initials P.R.B.
stops.quote_source: William Holman Hunt, Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (Macmillan, 1905), chapter VIII synopsis; a contents line, not verified as running prose
suggested_refs: The four issues of The Germ, January to April 1850

stops.name: Hogsmill River, Ewell: the hireling shepherd
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1851; the month is the working season, not a documented date
stops.campa: He goes down to the Hogsmill at Ewell in the summer of 1851 and paints The Hireling Shepherd out of doors, leaf by leaf, on the bank. Millais is at the same water painting Ophelia. It is the parish where a clerk misspelled his mother's name at his baptism; the river runs past that church. A local woman the group calls the Coptic sits for the shepherdess. The two pictures made in one Surrey summer on one stretch of water become the standard proof of what the Brotherhood meant by painting from nature.
suggested_refs: The stretch of the Hogsmill at Ewell where Hunt painted The Hireling Shepherd and Millais painted Ophelia

stops.name: Worcester Park Farm, the lantern painted by night
stops.date_confidence: contested. Wikipedia names three rival locations for the first Light of the World: a hut at Worcester Park Farm, the garden of the Oxford University Press, and a site near Bethlehem. None is preferred here. The picture is dated 1849/1850 to 1854.
stops.campa: Somewhere in these years he paints a man with a lantern knocking at a door that has no handle on his side. Where he paints it is not settled: a makeshift hut at Worcester Park Farm, working by night to get the lamplight right; or the garden of the Oxford University Press; or a site near Bethlehem. The three accounts sit in the record side by side and none of them yields. The picture is finished in 1853 and shown at the Academy in 1854, and no dispute about its address has ever slowed it down.
suggested_refs: Worcester Park Farm, Surrey, one of three claimed sites of the first Light of the World

stops.name: Prospect Place, Chelsea: the studio years
stops.date_confidence: attested to the decade; Wikipedia gives the Prospect Place studio as 1850s without months
stops.campa: He works from a home studio at Prospect Place in Chelsea, the row later renumbered into Cheyne Walk. Out of these rooms come Our English Coasts in 1852 and The Awakening Conscience in 1853, a kept woman rising from her keeper's knee in a furnished room where every object is new and nothing in it is hers. The same year he paints the picture titled Dante Gabriel Rossetti at 22 Years of Age; the sitter is in fact twenty-five, the title being a title and not a record. He is engaged in this decade to the model Annie Miller, and the engagement fails.
stops.quote: The true limner has to show the hideousness and deadliness of sham fascination by proving the everlasting dignity of the natural proportions of the human form.
stops.quote_source: William Holman Hunt, Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (Macmillan, 1905), Preface
suggested_refs: Prospect Place, Chelsea, later renumbered into Cheyne Walk

stops.name: Royal Academy, the lantern shown
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; May is the Academy's exhibition month
stops.campa: The Light of the World hangs at the Academy in 1854 and begins the second career of an English picture: not admired, used. It is engraved, hung in parlours and mission halls, carried into schoolrooms across the empire. In 1873 Martha Combe gives the first version to Keble College, Oxford, after her husband's death. Hunt will paint it twice more across the next fifty years. Nothing else he makes will travel as far, and he is twenty-seven when the first one leaves his hands.
stops.quote: To whom but the artist is relegated the task of giving a tangible and worthy image of the national body and mind, who else may select and uphold the visible sign of that beauty in his race which is most heroic physically and mentally ?
stops.quote_source: William Holman Hunt, Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (Macmillan, 1905), Preface, pp. xiii-xiv; quoted in full, the short form in circulation being a truncation
suggested_refs: The first version of The Light of the World, Royal Academy exhibition of 1854
sources: William Holman Hunt, Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (1905), Internet Archive scan preraphaelitism01hunt

stops.name: Paris, the road to the packet
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source reached this session states any Hunt event in Paris; the Paris and Marseille legs are the ordinary mid-century route to Egypt, inferred from the period rather than from his record. Canonical atlas pin inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: He leaves England in the winter of 1854 for reasons he gives as religious: he wants the actual topography and the actual faces, having decided that a painter of scripture who has not stood in the country of scripture is guessing. The route is the ordinary one of the age, Paris and then a Mediterranean packet out of Marseille, and it is a route reconstructed from the period's habits rather than from anything he left. Nothing reached this session states a single event of his in the city.
suggested_refs: The Paris to Marseille rail and packet route to Alexandria in the 1850s
sources: General account of the 1854 Holy Land journey in Hunt biographies; port and route not independently confirmed
Canonical Paris pin inherited from the atlas

stops.name: Alexandria, the landing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the port of entry is the standard account and is not confirmed by any source reached
stops.campa: The steamer puts him ashore at Alexandria, the gate through which Europe enters the east in the eighteen-fifties. The port of entry is what the general accounts give and not what any document reached this session confirms. What is certain is that from this coast onward he means to draw every biblical face from a living model in the country the Bible names. He is a Protestant Englishman about to spend two years hunting the historical Jesus with a brush.
suggested_refs: The Alexandria packet quay, standard European entry to Egypt in the 1850s
sources: General account of the 1854 journey; port of entry not independently confirmed this session

stops.name: Old Cairo, the Coptic quarter and the pyramids
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Cairo and Giza weeks rest on the general biographical account, with no source reached this session documenting a day of them
stops.campa: He spends weeks in Cairo and goes into the Coptic quarter, studying the costume and the features of a Christian community established in Egypt since before Constantine and looking nothing like the Christians of English altarpieces. He rides out to the pyramids and the Sphinx at Giza, as nearly every European traveller of the decade does. All of this rests on the general account; no source reached documents it. The word Coptic will come back three years later in Surrey, as a nickname for a shepherdess.
suggested_refs: The Coptic quarter of Old Cairo and the Giza plateau, standard stations of the Victorian eastern tour
sources: General account of Hunt's 1854 Egyptian sojourn; not independently confirmed this session

stops.name: Jaffa Gate, the entry into Jerusalem
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the arrival is attested, the gate is not
stops.campa: He comes up from Egypt overland and enters the city by the Jaffa Gate on the western side, where the road from the coast arrives. Which gate is tradition rather than record. Jerusalem in 1854 is an Ottoman provincial town of some fifteen thousand people inside its walls, filling with European consulates and missions, and the Crimean war has just opened a thousand miles to the north. He has come to paint the place as it is, on the working theory that as it is and as it was are close enough.
suggested_refs: The Jaffa Gate of the Old City, the western arrival for travellers from the coast
sources: General account of Hunt's 1854 arrival in Jerusalem; specific gate not independently confirmed

stops.name: Haram al-Sharif, the ground at the centre
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of presence in the city only. No source reached states that Hunt entered the Haram; the pin is inherited unchanged from the atlas, where it stands for Muhammad's night journey.
stops.campa: At the middle of the walled city stands the platform the atlas already pins for Muhammad, carried here by night from Mecca and ascending from the rock. Nothing reached this session says Hunt went up onto it, and a Protestant Englishman in 1854 would not have been admitted in any case. He works around it, in the streets and outside the walls. The geography he has crossed a continent to measure is geography two other faiths have been mapping for twelve hundred years. The pin is inherited here, not earned.
suggested_refs: The Haram al-Sharif platform, already pinned in the atlas for the Night Journey
sources: General account of Hunt's Jerusalem residence

stops.name: Jerusalem, the house he builds
stops.date_confidence: the fact of the house is attested by Wikipedia; its address, and the year it was built, are not given in anything reached
stops.campa: He does not lodge and leave. He builds a house in Jerusalem and works from it, a studio in the city itself, which he will use again on two later journeys. It is the practical form of the argument: not a sketching tour but a residence, on the ground that a painter of this material ought to live inside the material. The house is attested; its address is not given in anything reached. From it he goes out to the Dead Sea, to Bethlehem, into the hills, and comes back to finish.
suggested_refs: Hunt's own house in Jerusalem, base of three journeys; address not established
sources: Wikipedia, 'William Holman Hunt' ('He eventually built his own house in Jerusalem')

stops.name: Jerusalem, Henry Wentworth Monk
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1854; the month is not given
stops.campa: In Jerusalem he meets Henry Wentworth Monk, a Canadian millenarian who has come to the city to wait for the end of the age and to argue for the return of the Jews to Palestine. Monk reads the scapegoat of Leviticus as a figure of Christ, driven out bearing what is not its own. Hunt takes the reading and will build a painting on it. He is at this point still at The Finding of the Saviour in the Temple and cannot get Jewish models to sit for him; the picture stalls where it stands.
stops.quote: Am driven to abandon picture and determine to paint 'The Scapegoat'.
stops.quote_source: William Holman Hunt, Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (Macmillan, 1905), chapter XVI synopsis; a contents line, not verified as running prose
suggested_refs: Henry Wentworth Monk in Jerusalem, 1854, and his reading of Leviticus 16

stops.name: Mount Sodom, the goat on the salt
stops.date_confidence: attested to the autumn of 1854 by Hunt's own Royal Academy catalogue note; the month is the working season
stops.campa: He goes down to the Dead Sea and sets up on the salt crust at Sodom, the mountains of Edom across the water, and paints a white goat dying on the shore with a red fillet on its horns. He works under threat from raiding parties and says afterwards that most of the canvas was done on the spot. The atlas already stands on this plain for Abraham, who watches the cities burn from above it. Hunt paints the same ground as the place where a nation puts its sins outside the camp and lets them walk away.
suggested_refs: The salt margin at Usdum on the Dead Sea, where most of The Scapegoat was painted on site
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Scapegoat (painting)', citing Hunt's Royal Academy catalogue note
abraham.journey.json, stops 'The Dead Sea plain' and 'The Dead Sea'

stops.name: Bethlehem, the third claim
stops.date_confidence: contested. Wikipedia lists a site near Bethlehem as one of three rival candidate locations for the painting of the first Light of the World, alongside Worcester Park Farm and the Oxford University Press garden. The dispute is unresolved and is not resolved here.
stops.campa: Six miles south of Jerusalem, at Bethlehem, he studies the dawn light. One of the three accounts of where the first Light of the World was painted puts the work here rather than at Worcester Park Farm or in the Oxford University Press garden, and the three have never been reconciled. The stop is entered because the dispute is part of the record, not because this limb of it is preferred. He is in the country either way, and the dispute is over a hut, a garden and a hillside, none of which the picture names.
suggested_refs: The hills outside Bethlehem, one of three claimed sites of the first Light of the World

stops.name: London, the return and the goat exhibited
stops.date_confidence: the 1856 exhibition is attested; the return route and date are a gap, unrecorded in anything reached
stops.campa: He comes back to London by a route no source reached this session records, finishes The Scapegoat in his studio, touches it up into 1856, and hangs it at the Academy that year. The public does not know what to do with it. Two versions exist, the smaller now at Manchester, the larger at the Lady Lever Gallery in Port Sunlight. He has been away two years, and what he has brought home is a picture of an animal dying on a beach, painted mostly on that beach.
suggested_refs: The two versions of The Scapegoat, Manchester Art Gallery and the Lady Lever Art Gallery, Port Sunlight

stops.name: London, the Firm founded without him
stops.date_confidence: the founding date and partner list are attested in three atlas files; Hunt's absence is a documented absence, not an inference about his whereabouts
stops.campa: On the eleventh of April 1861 Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Company opens for business, and its partners are William Morris, Rossetti, Edward Burne-Jones, Philip Webb, Ford Madox Brown, Marshall and Faulkner. Hunt is not among them. Four years earlier the Oxford Union murals were painted by Rossetti, Morris and Burne-Jones, and Jane Burden and her sister Bessie Burden were taken as models there; Hunt is not recorded in that room either. The Brotherhood he founded acquires a second life, and it forms around Rossetti.
suggested_refs: The founding partnership of Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co., 11 April 1861

stops.name: London, the marriage to Fanny Waugh
stops.date_confidence: contested and partly resolved. The DNB 1912 supplement gives 1865; the Wikipedia summary gives 1861 and is treated as an error. The widely repeated day, 28 December, could not be confirmed against any register reached, so only the year is asserted.
stops.campa: In 1864 he paints London Bridge on the Night of the Marriage of the Prince and Princess of Wales, a crowd under gaslight. In 1865 he marries Fanny Waugh. The year comes from the Dictionary of National Biography; a Wikipedia summary says 1861 and is wrong; the day, repeated everywhere as the twenty-eighth of December, could not be confirmed against any register reached, and is withheld. He is thirty-eight, and has been exhibiting for eighteen years.
suggested_refs: The marriage register of Hunt and Fanny Waugh, 1865; the exact day remains unconfirmed
sources: Dictionary of National Biography, 1912 supplement, 'Hunt, William Holman'
Wikipedia, 'William Holman Hunt' (giving 1861, recorded as a contradiction)

stops.name: Florence, the son born
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the birth of Cyril Benoni Holman Hunt in Florence in October 1866 rests on standard biographies and was not confirmed by a source fetched this session
stops.campa: The couple travel to Italy in 1866, bound eventually for the east. Fanny sits for Isabella, leaning over the pot of basil in which a murdered lover's head is buried. In October, in Florence, she gives birth to a son, Cyril Benoni Holman Hunt. Benoni is a name out of Genesis: son of my sorrow, what Rachel calls her child as she dies bearing him. The birth is given by the standard biographies and by no source reached this session. The naming stands in the record without a gloss from him.
suggested_refs: Cyril Benoni Holman Hunt, born Florence, October 1866
sources: Standard Hunt biographies; not independently confirmed via a source fetched this session

stops.name: Florence, the fever
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1866; the day is not given in anything reached and the 20th is a placeholder inside the month
stops.campa: In December Fanny dies in Florence of a fever following the birth, some weeks after it. It is not, as is often written, a death in childbirth; the sources say fever after giving birth, and the distinction is the difference between an hour and a month. Hunt is left in a foreign city with an infant and a body. He has been married one year. The journey east is abandoned where it stands, and he stays on in Tuscany to do the only thing he knows how to do with a fact, which is make an object out of it.
suggested_refs: The death of Fanny Holman Hunt at Florence, December 1866
sources: Wikipedia, 'Isabella and the Pot of Basil'

stops.name: Fiesole, the tomb cut
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1866-1867 without months; January is a placeholder
stops.campa: He goes up to Fiesole above the city and carves his wife's tomb himself, a painter working stone for the first and last time, before it is brought down into Florence for burial. Nothing reached this session says how long the work takes him or who assists. What is attested is that he cut it with his own hands rather than commissioning it, in a country full of monumental masons who would have done it faster and cheaper. He is thirty-nine, a widower with a son three months old, and what he makes that winter is a tomb.
suggested_refs: Hunt's carved tomb for Fanny, made at Fiesole

stops.name: Piazzale Donatello, the English Cemetery and the chalice
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1867 and after; months are not given
stops.campa: The tomb is set in the English Cemetery on the Piazzale Donatello, the walled island for Protestant dead in a Catholic city, a few paces from Elizabeth Barrett Browning, who has lain there since 1861. Hunt keeps his connection to St Mark's, the English church on Via Maggio, and pays for a communion chalice inscribed to Fanny's memory. Two objects, a stone he cut and a cup he bought, are what he leaves in Florence. He will come back to the city; he does not move his life there.
suggested_refs: The English Cemetery, Piazzale Donatello, Florence, and St Mark's English Church, Via Maggio

stops.name: London, Isabella finished after the sitter
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: Back in London he finishes Isabella and the Pot of Basil in 1868, and The Birthday the same year. The Isabella is the picture his wife sat for in Florence; he completes it after her death, a woman bent over a pot with a murdered head buried in it, and it goes out into the world as a subject from Keats. Between the sitting and the varnish the model has died of fever in a foreign city and been buried under a stone the painter cut himself. None of that appears in the catalogue entry.
suggested_refs: Isabella and the Pot of Basil (1868), for which Fanny Waugh sat before her death
sources: Wikipedia, 'Isabella and the Pot of Basil'

stops.name: Old Cairo, the second going out
stops.date_confidence: the DNB gives a landing at Jaffa in autumn 1869; the Cairo leg is the general account and is not confirmed by any source reached
stops.campa: Three years a widower, he goes east again by Cairo, on the same programme: the actual country, the actual faces, for pictures the English will hang in rooms that have never seen it. The Dictionary of National Biography puts his landing at Jaffa in the autumn of 1869. The Cairo leg rests on the general account rather than on a document reached this session. He is forty-two, and this is the second of three journeys that will take, between them, something close to eight years out of his working life.
suggested_refs: The autumn 1869 landing at Jaffa, opening the second Holy Land journey
sources: Dictionary of National Biography, 1912 supplement, 'Hunt, William Holman'
General account of the return to the Near East c. 1869

stops.name: Jerusalem, the second residence
stops.date_confidence: 1869 to 1871 per the DNB, correcting the 1872 that circulates. Whether he travelled to Nazareth in these years is unresolved in everything reached and is left open.
stops.campa: He reopens the house in Jerusalem and works from it until 1871, painting religious subjects on the ground that gave them their names. Whether he travelled up to Nazareth in these years, or built its carpenter's shop in the Jerusalem studio out of study and inference, is not settled by anything reached this session and is left open. The Dictionary of National Biography gives the return as 1871, against the 1872 that circulates; the earlier date sits better with what he brings home.
suggested_refs: Hunt's Jerusalem house during the second sojourn, 1869 to 1871
sources: Dictionary of National Biography, 1912 supplement, 'Hunt, William Holman'
General account of the second Holy Land sojourn; Nazareth visit unconfirmed

stops.name: London, The Shadow of Death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: The Shadow of Death is finished in 1873: a carpenter straightening his back at dusk in a Nazareth workshop, arms out, the shadow thrown onto the tool rack behind him in the shape of a cross he has not yet been given. The public takes it as it did not take the goat. Every plank and every tool in it has been studied from the country it depicts, which is the point of the years he has just spent abroad and the only justification he offers for having spent them.
suggested_refs: The Shadow of Death (1873), painted after the second Holy Land journey

stops.name: Neuchatel, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1875; the day is not given
stops.campa: Marriage to a deceased wife's sister is illegal in England, so in November 1875 he takes Fanny's younger sister Edith Waugh across to Neuchatel, in francophone Switzerland, and marries her there. The English law will not change for another thirty-two years. Thomas Woolner, one of the seven who signed the Brotherhood into being at Gower Street, breaks with him over it, and so do members of the family. He is forty-eight, and he has arranged his second marriage the way he arranges his pictures, by going to the place where the thing is possible.
suggested_refs: The Deceased Wife's Sister's Marriage Act 1907, which legalised in England what Hunt went to Switzerland for in 1875

stops.name: Jerusalem, the third residence
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the third journey is given as c. 1875 to 1878 by the general account, and the itinerary beyond Cairo and Jerusalem is a gap
stops.campa: He goes east a third time, with Edith, by way of Cairo, and works again from the Jerusalem house toward The Triumph of the Innocents, the Holy Family on the flight into Egypt walking accompanied by the ghosts of the children Herod killed in their place. Recurring illness troubles him through the period. The itinerary beyond Cairo and Jerusalem is not established by anything reached this session, and the dates 1875 to 1878 are the general account rather than a document.
suggested_refs: The Triumph of the Innocents, begun on the third Near Eastern journey
sources: General account of Hunt's third Near Eastern journey; not independently confirmed via a source fetched this session

stops.name: Mar Elias, the bench between two cities
stops.date_confidence: the painting site and the bench are attested; the bench is undated in every source reached, and which wife placed it is not stated. 1877 marks the working period, not the bench.
stops.campa: On the hill road between Jerusalem and Bethlehem stands the monastery of Mar Elias, looking south over Bethlehem and the Herodium. Hunt paints major work at this spot. Facing the monastery a stone bench is set up by his wife, cut with verses of scripture in Hebrew, Greek, Arabic and English, four alphabets on one seat. Neither the year of the bench nor which of the two wives placed it is given in anything reached. Edith outlived him, which points at her and does not prove her.
suggested_refs: The inscribed stone bench facing Mar Elias Monastery, erected by Hunt's wife

stops.name: London, the return and the Triumph
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the 1878 return is the general account and the exact date is a gap
stops.campa: He comes home in 1878, on a date the sources reached do not fix, and finishes The Triumph of the Innocents in a London studio. It closes the programme he began in 1854: twenty-four years, three journeys east, and a house in Jerusalem kept between them. What he claimed for these pictures was that the light in them had been measured where the events happened, and this is the last one he can claim it for. He is fifty-one. He will paint for another twenty-six years and never go east again.
suggested_refs: The Triumph of the Innocents, completed in London after the third journey
sources: General account of Hunt's career; exact return date not independently confirmed this session

stops.name: London, Amaryllis and the Magdalen dawn
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1884 and 1890; May is the month of the Magdalen ceremony depicted, not a documented painting date
stops.campa: Amaryllis in 1884, and in 1890 May Morning on Magdalen Tower: the Oxford choristers singing the sun up on the first of May from the top of the tower, a medieval usage kept alive by a college. He is in his sixties and painting ceremonies rather than arguments. The Brotherhood is long dissolved, Rossetti is dead of chloral, Millais will end as president of the Academy the seven of them set out to overthrow, and Hunt is the one still doing precisely what he said in 1848 he would do.
suggested_refs: May Morning on Magdalen Tower (1890), Oxford

stops.name: 18 Melbury Road, the house and the third lantern
stops.date_confidence: the third version is dated 1900 to 1904; the move to Melbury Road is dated 1903. Coordinate corrected to 51.4992, -0.2022, the three conflicting values in the research pool all being wrong.
stops.campa: In Holland Park, among the purpose-built studio houses of the late Victorian painters, he takes 18 Melbury Road as residence and studio and lives there to the end. From 1900 to 1904 he paints The Light of the World a third time, life-sized, fifty years after the first. Glaucoma and age have taken his eyes; Edward Robert Hughes works at the canvas under his direction. The man who founded a movement on painting exactly what he saw finishes his last picture by telling another man what to put down.
suggested_refs: 18 Melbury Road, Holland Park, Hunt's final house and studio

stops.name: London, the autobiography and the Order of Merit
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month of neither the publication nor the appointment is given
stops.campa: In 1905 he publishes Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in two volumes, and Edward VII appoints him to the Order of Merit. He is the last founder standing and he writes the history accordingly: fifty-seven years after Gower Street, the account of what the seven meant is given by the only one of them left to give it. Every later account of that September in Bloomsbury runs through this book, which is a memoir and is handled by scholars as a document.
stops.quote: Art, as of old, should stamp a nation's individuality; it should be the witness of its life to all eternity.
stops.quote_source: William Holman Hunt, Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (Macmillan, 1905), Preface
suggested_refs: Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (Macmillan, 1905), 2 vols.
sources: William Holman Hunt, Pre-Raphaelitism and the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (1905), Internet Archive scan preraphaelitism01hunt

stops.name: St Paul's Cathedral, the dedication after the world tour
stops.date_confidence: the 1908 dedication and the 1905 to 1907 tour are attested; the month of the dedication is not given. The Australian viewing figure is a period claim, not a measured statistic.
stops.campa: The life-sized third version tours the world from 1905 to 1907, drawing crowds; of Australia it was claimed at the time that four-fifths of the population saw it, a period figure and not a measured one. Charles Booth, shipowner and social investigator of London poverty, gives the picture to St Paul's, and it is dedicated there in 1908. Hunt is eighty-one and nearly blind. The painting he began by lamplight in his twenties comes to rest in the cathedral of the capital.
suggested_refs: The third Light of the World in St Paul's Cathedral, given by Charles Booth and dedicated 1908

stops.name: 18 Melbury Road, the last of the seven
stops.date_confidence: attested. The DNB gives the place of death as 18 Melbury Road, Kensington, closing the Kensington versus Sonning-on-Thames confusion carried in the research pool.
stops.campa: He dies at his residence, 18 Melbury Road, Kensington, on the seventh of September 1910, aged eighty-three. The Dictionary of National Biography states the place, which closes a long-standing confusion between the Kensington house and Sonning-on-Thames. He is the last of the seven. Rossetti died in 1882, Woolner in 1892, Millais in 1896. The movement he named at Gower Street sixty-two years earlier has become the standard English picture of the Middle Ages, and he outlives everyone who started it.
suggested_refs: The death notice of William Holman Hunt, 18 Melbury Road, Kensington, 7 September 1910
sources: Dictionary of National Biography, 1912 supplement, 'Hunt, William Holman'

stops.name: St Paul's Cathedral, Golders Green and the crypt
stops.date_confidence: the cremation at Golders Green and the interment of the ashes in the crypt are attested by the DNB; the day is not given, and the 14th is a placeholder after the death
stops.campa: He is cremated at Golders Green and his ashes are interred in the crypt of St Paul's Cathedral, a few hundred yards from the Cheapside street where he was born. St Paul's own published history and collections material, checked directly, describes the painting hanging above and says nothing at all about the ashes below; the interment is recorded by the Dictionary of National Biography. The exact day is not given in anything reached. He lies under the building his last picture stands in.
suggested_refs: The crypt of St Paul's Cathedral, where Hunt's ashes were interred after cremation at Golders Green
sources: Dictionary of National Biography, 1912 supplement, 'Hunt, William Holman'
St Paul's Cathedral, 'History and Collections', checked and found silent on the burial

stops.name: Keble College, Oxford: the three versions dispersed
stops.date_confidence: the Keble donation is dated 1873, the library placement 1878, the move to the purpose-built side chapel 1892 to 1895, and the Manchester purchase 1912. Coordinate corrected to 51.7589, -1.2577, the pool's value falling about 600 m north-west of the college.
stops.campa: Martha Combe gives the first Light of the World to Keble College in 1873, after her husband Thomas Combe's death. It sits in the library from 1878 and moves into a purpose-built side chapel between 1892 and 1895, where it stays. Two years after Hunt dies, Manchester buys the smaller second version, painted between 1851 and 1856, into a municipal collection raised by a cotton city for its own public; the same gallery holds the smaller of the two Scapegoats. One picture painted three times over fifty years ends in an Oxford college, a Manchester gallery, and the cathedral a few streets from where he was born.
suggested_refs: The side chapel at Keble College, Oxford, built 1892-95 to house The Light of the World
The second version of The Light of the World, Manchester Art Gallery, purchased 1912

stops.name: 18 Melbury Road, the plaque and the afterimage
stops.date_confidence: the plaque year is attested; the later items are dated to their own years. That Diana Holman-Hunt's book displaced the public image is a reconstruction, not stated in any entry fetched.
stops.campa: In 1923 a blue plaque goes up on the house in Melbury Road. In 1969 his granddaughter Diana Holman-Hunt publishes My Grandfather, His Wives and Loves, a domestic account of the two Waugh sisters and the marriages, and the intimate Hunt of that book crowds out the public one he built in 1905, although nothing reached this session states so in as many words. In 2009 the BBC casts Rafe Spall as him in Desperate Romantics, thirty-four years after The Love School had done it first.
suggested_refs: Diana Holman-Hunt, My Grandfather, His Wives and Loves (1969)
Desperate Romantics, BBC Two, 21 July to 25 August 2009
